after: ## What a thesis already tells the reader
alt: Three versions of a thesis on free public transport, each longer than the last: a claim only; a claim with a governing reason (fares work against the purpose of the service); and a claim with a preview of three reasons (fares exclude riders, consume what they raise, keep drivers in cars).
caption: A preview is an indication of structure, not a table of contents.

alt: Three thesis versions checked against three tests. The announcement (“This essay will look at fares...”) and the bare list fail to take a position, say what the effect is, or offer something to argue with. The preview (“Free transport would repair three failures...”) passes all three.
caption: A preview makes a claim and signals reasons; an announcement and a list do neither.

alt: Four small diagrams of how a thesis signals structure: parallel reasons (a claim branching to A, B and C), a progression (rising steps), a contrast or concession (X acknowledged, then Y), and a sequence of effects (first, then, finally). Below, an analysis thesis that previews two stages of a speech.
caption: Reasons, progression, concession or sequence: the thesis tells the reader what shape to expect.

after: ## Worked example 2: reading a thesis for its signals
alt: The perennials thesis names three reasons, cost, insects and water, each colour-coded and linked by an arrow to the body paragraph that develops it, in the same order, with “first” and “finally” marking the sequence.
caption: Measure each paragraph against the promise the thesis makes.

after: ## Weak, better and strong theses for an analysis
alt: Three thesis versions for analysing a captain’s speech to a rowing team: weak (“uses ethos, pathos and logos”), better (“motivates the team by appealing to their emotions”) and strong (moves from what the team has endured to what is still to be earned, converting weariness into pride).
caption: A strong analysis thesis previews the speech’s movement and its effect.
